headline: Fewer abnormal heartbeats, more deaths?
title: Preliminary report: effect of encainide and flecainide on mortality in a randomized trial of arrhythmia suppression after myocardial infarction
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: CAST enrolled heart attack survivors whose extra heartbeats could be suppressed with medication, then randomized their treatment. More patients died in the groups receiving encainide or flecainide, and those parts of the trial were stopped early.

headline: If almost no antibody could be left, what are the cells reacting to?
title: Human basophil degranulation triggered by very dilute antiserum against IgE
note: Researchers reported that an extremely dilute antibody preparation still made human immune cells called basophils release their granules. The paper became central to the controversy over whether water has a memory. A later Nature study tested the claim and did not reproduce degranulation at the very high dilutions. https://doi.org/10.1038/366525a0

headline: Can a nursery night-light leave a child nearsighted?
title: Myopia and ambient lighting at night
note: Researchers asked parents at an eye clinic how brightly lit their children's bedrooms had been before age two. Children who had slept in brighter rooms were more likely to be nearsighted later. Two follow-up reports in Nature did not recover the original night-light association. Parental myopia was identified as relevant because it was also associated with nursery-light use. https://doi.org/10.1038/35004661 https://doi.org/10.1038/35004663

headline: Can a pill improve cholesterol numbers and still lead to more deaths?
title: Effects of Torcetrapib in Patients at High Risk for Coronary Events
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The randomized trial found that torcetrapib raised HDL and lowered LDL while increasing cardiovascular events and deaths. The trial was stopped early.

headline: Could getting ICU blood sugar closer to normal make more patients die?
title: Intensive versus Conventional Glucose Control in Critically Ill Patients
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: In NICE-SUGAR, the intensive-target group had higher 90-day mortality and more severe hypoglycemia. An earlier single-center surgical ICU trial had reported lower mortality with intensive insulin therapy. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa011300

headline: Does washing out an arthritic knee do more than making a few skin incisions?
title: A controlled trial of arthroscopic surgery for osteoarthritis of the knee
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Patients with knee osteoarthritis received arthroscopic cleaning, a joint washout, or sham surgery. Over two years, neither procedure beat the sham operation on pain or function.

headline: Did the survival advantage of activated protein C survive a later trial?
title: Drotrecogin Alfa (Activated) in Adults with Septic Shock
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The later PROWESS-SHOCK trial did not detect a mortality benefit at 28 or 90 days. An earlier trial in severe sepsis had reported lower mortality. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200103083441001

headline: Does an Oscar come with four extra years of life?
title: Survival in Academy Award-winning actors and actresses
note: Researchers reported that Oscar-winning actors lived about four years longer than actors who appeared in the same films. To enter the winners' group, an actor first had to survive long enough to collect the award. A reanalysis accounting for the time actors had to survive in order to win found a smaller estimated survival difference, with uncertainty including no difference. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16954361/

headline: Does a stent beat a sham procedure for exercise time in stable angina?
title: Percutaneous coronary intervention in stable angina (ORBITA): a double-blind, randomised controlled trial
note: In patients receiving optimized medication, this blinded trial did not detect a significant difference in exercise time between stenting and sham. A later placebo-controlled trial with little or no antianginal medication and a different primary outcome reported symptom benefit. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2310610

headline: Does targeting kidney nerves lower blood pressure more than a sham procedure?
title: A Controlled Trial of Renal Denervation for Resistant Hypertension
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: An earlier open-label trial reported large office blood pressure reductions. This blinded sham-controlled trial did not find a significant six-month difference in its primary blood pressure outcome. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21093036/

headline: Did a vitamin C cocktail look lifesaving before it was randomized?
title: Effect of Vitamin C, Hydrocortisone, and Thiamine vs Hydrocortisone Alone on Time Alive and Free of Vasopressor Support Among Patients With Septic Shock: The VITAMINS Randomized Clinical Trial
note: A retrospective before-and-after study had reported a large mortality difference. This randomized comparison found no improvement in its primary outcome of time alive and off medication supporting blood pressure. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27940189/

headline: Did IV vitamin C make a sepsis trial's main outcome worse?
title: Intravenous Vitamin C in Adults with Sepsis in the Intensive Care Unit
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The primary composite of death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days occurred more often in the vitamin C group than in the placebo group.

headline: If produce looks good for the lungs, will beta carotene in a pill help too?
title: The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: In a randomized trial of Finnish men who smoked, lung cancer incidence was 18% higher among those assigned beta carotene supplements than among those who did not receive beta carotene.

headline: Does shaving bone from a sore shoulder beat putting a camera in for a look?
title: Arthroscopic subacromial decompression for subacromial shoulder pain (CSAW): a multicentre, pragmatic, parallel group, placebo-controlled, three-group, randomised surgical trial
note: Patients with pain beneath the tip of the shoulder received decompression surgery, a camera-only procedure, or no treatment. At six months, shoulder function scores did not differ significantly between the two surgical groups.

headline: Does trimming a torn meniscus make a difference patients can feel?
title: Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery for a degenerative meniscal tear
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Patients had a degenerative tear in the inner knee cartilage and no knee osteoarthritis. A year later, symptoms and function had improved by similar amounts after partial removal of the meniscus and after sham surgery.

headline: Does bone cement ease the pain of a fractured vertebra?
title: A randomized trial of vertebroplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Patients with painful spinal fractures from osteoporosis received a bone cement injection or a sham procedure. Both groups reported less pain. The differences between groups were not significant at any assessment through six months.

headline: Would hospital visits have dropped anyway in a program for frequent patients?
title: Health Care Hotspotting: A Randomized, Controlled Trial
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Hospital readmissions fell after enrollment, but the randomized comparison found a similar 180-day readmission rate in the intervention and usual-care groups. A before-and-after comparison alone would have looked favorable.

headline: Can a fake inhaler make breathing feel better without improving airflow?
title: Active Albuterol or Placebo, Sham Acupuncture, or No Intervention in Asthma
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Self-reported improvement was similar with albuterol, a placebo inhaler, and sham acupuncture. Only albuterol produced the larger improvement in the objective measure of lung function.

headline: Did tying off chest arteries relieve angina better than making the incisions alone?
title: An Evaluation of Internal-Mammary-Artery Ligation by a Double-Blind Technic
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: A small historical trial compared artery ligation with sham operations. Symptom improvement occurred in both groups. A subsequent sham-controlled study likewise found no advantage for ligation. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13816818/

headline: Did Germany's World Cup matches send more people into cardiac emergencies?
title: Cardiovascular Events during World Cup Soccer
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The Munich-area study reported 2.66 times as many cardiovascular emergencies on Germany's match days as in control periods. A later study using hospital records for the same World Cup across Bavaria did not find a significant increase. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24182671/

headline: Can duct tape beat freezing for common warts?
title: The Efficacy of Duct Tape vs Cryotherapy in the Treatment of Verruca Vulgaris (the Common Wart)
note: This small trial reported more wart resolution with duct tape than cryotherapy. A later placebo-controlled trial in schoolchildren using a different tape protocol did not detect a statistically significant difference. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17088514/

headline: Can lowering blood sugar more aggressively lead to more deaths even outside the ICU?
title: Effects of Intensive Glucose Lowering in Type 2 Diabetes
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The ACCORD intensive-treatment arm was stopped early because mortality was higher. The primary cardiovascular composite had not been significantly reduced.

headline: Did freezing the inside of the stomach treat ulcers better than a sham procedure?
title: A Cooperative Double-Blind Evaluation of Gastric Freezing in the Treatment of Duodenal Ulcer
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Investigators compared gastric freezing with a control procedure in a double-blind evaluation. The trial did not show a clinical advantage for freezing. Ulcer complications had also been reported. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM196405072701908

headline: Vitamin E users had fewer heart problems. Would handing out the pills do the same?
title: Vitamin E consumption and the risk of coronary disease in women
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: A study following female nurses found that long-term users of vitamin E supplements had a lower risk of major coronary disease.

headline: Did a vitamin E pill meant to prevent cancer produce more prostate cancer diagnoses?
title: Vitamin E and the Risk of Prostate Cancer: The Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
note: Longer follow-up of the randomized prevention trial found a higher incidence of prostate cancer in the vitamin E-only group than in the placebo group.

headline: Do some heart patients fare better when cardiologists are away at a conference?
title: Mortality and Treatment Patterns Among Patients Hospitalized With Acute Cardiovascular Conditions During Dates of National Cardiology Meetings
note: This observational analysis found lower adjusted 30-day mortality among high-risk heart failure and cardiac arrest patients admitted to teaching hospitals during meeting dates. High-risk heart attack mortality was similar across dates. The exposure was the conference calendar.

headline: For a kidney stone on a roller coaster, is the back seat better?
title: Validation of a Functional Pyelocalyceal Renal Model for the Evaluation of Renal Calculi Passage While Riding a Roller Coaster
venue: The Journal of the American Osteopathic Association
note: Researchers took a model kidney holding real stones on a roller coaster. Stones were more likely to leave the small cup-shaped chambers of the model when it rode in the back. The experiment measured stones moving inside a model, with no patients aboard as study subjects.

headline: Can bee stings make multiple sclerosis better?
title: A randomized crossover study of bee sting therapy for multiple sclerosis
note: This crossover trial found no reduction in new MRI lesions or improvements in disability, fatigue, or quality of life with bee sting therapy.

headline: Can drinking a pig parasite's eggs improve ulcerative colitis symptoms?
title: Trichuris suis therapy for active ulcerative colitis: a randomized controlled trial
note: More participants met the trial's threshold for clinical improvement in the parasite-egg group than with placebo. The difference in the remission outcome was not statistically clear.

headline: Do leeches beat an anti-inflammatory gel for knee pain?
title: Effectiveness of leech therapy in osteoarthritis of the knee: a randomized, controlled trial
note: The small trial reported greater short-term pain improvement with leeches than with topical diclofenac. Patients could tell which treatment they received.

headline: Were patients admitted on weekends more likely to die in the hospital?
title: Mortality among Patients Admitted to Hospitals on Weekends as Compared with Weekdays
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The registry analysis reported higher adjusted mortality for some diagnoses among weekend emergency admissions. Later work examined how much selection and differences in illness severity could explain the association. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6245775/

headline: Can putting a brand name on a dummy pill make a headache feel better?
title: Analgesic effects of branding in treatment of headaches
note: The trial crossed branded and unbranded packaging with aspirin and placebo. Participants rated headache relief higher overall with branded tablets. In the placebo comparison the tablets had the same inactive contents.

headline: Can chewing gum prevent ear infections?
title: Xylitol chewing gum in prevention of acute otitis media: double blind randomised trial
note: A daycare trial reported fewer acute middle-ear infections in children assigned xylitol gum than in those assigned sucrose gum. The comparison tested these gum formulations.

headline: Is Friday the 13th an unusually bad day for road injuries?
title: Is Friday the 13th bad for your health?
note: An exploratory comparison of Friday the 6th and Friday the 13th found less recorded traffic on the latter dates and more hospital admissions for transport accidents in its local sample.

headline: Does running a marathon make it harder for other people to reach emergency care?
title: Delays in Emergency Care and Mortality during Major U.S. Marathons
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: On marathon dates, emergency transport was slower in affected areas and older patients admitted with heart attack or cardiac arrest had higher observed 30-day mortality. The race-day comparison was observational.

headline: Can chilling your feet make you report a cold a few days later?
title: Acute cooling of the feet and the onset of common cold symptoms
note: More participants reported cold symptoms after a foot-cooling experiment than in the control group. The outcome was symptom reporting, with no laboratory confirmation of new infection.

headline: Can magnets in your shoes relieve heel pain better than fake magnets?
title: Effect of Magnetic vs Sham-Magnetic Insoles on Plantar Heel Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial
note: Pain improved in both groups with cushioned insoles. The magnetic inserts did not outperform otherwise comparable sham inserts.

headline: Can calling a migraine pill a placebo make the real drug work less well?
title: Altered placebo and drug labeling changes the outcome of episodic migraine attacks
note: The crossover trial varied both the migraine pill and its label. Reported pain relief depended on the label as well as whether the pill contained the drug.

headline: Can a placebo help with irritable bowel symptoms if the label admits it is a placebo?
title: Placebos without deception: a randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome
note: Patients knowingly receiving placebo pills reported better short-term symptoms than the no-treatment group. The trial used self-reported outcomes. A later trial compared open-label placebo, double-blind placebo, and no pills. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33605656/

headline: Are people more likely to die on their birthday?
title: Death has a preference for birthdays: an analysis of death time series
note: Swiss registry data showed an excess of recorded deaths on birthdays. This was an observational pattern across dates and causes of death.

headline: Did donor stool beat an antibiotic in a trial of recurrent C. difficile infection?
title: Duodenal Infusion of Donor Feces for Recurrent Clostridium difficile
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The trial stopped early after higher resolution rates with donor fecal infusion than with comparator regimens. This is an example of an unusual intervention supported by the randomized comparison. A subsequent trial compared donor and autologous material. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27547925/

headline: Can a stranger's prayer improve a patient's cardiac care chart?
title: A randomized, controlled trial of the effects of remote, intercessory prayer on outcomes in patients admitted to the coronary care unit
note: People prayed from a distance for patients on a list. Researchers scored each patient's hospital course from medical records. The prayer group had better scores, while the groups spent similar lengths of time in hospital.

headline: Can the phase of the moon predict visits for 58 diseases?
title: Assessment of effects of moon phases on hospital outpatient visits: An observational national study
note: Researchers compared outpatient records from Taiwanese health insurance data across lunar phases. They reported differences for 58 diagnostic categories.

headline: Does the full moon steal twenty minutes of your sleep?
title: Evidence that the lunar cycle influences human sleep
note: A retrospective analysis of laboratory sleep recordings reported shorter sleep and reduced EEG delta activity around the full moon.

headline: If you can feel my energy field, which hand am I holding mine over?
title: A close look at therapeutic touch
note: With a screen blocking their view, practitioners tried to tell whether the investigator held her hand above their left or right hand. Across 280 attempts, 21 practitioners picked correctly 44% of the time.

headline: Is surgery for a torn aorta more common near the full moon?
title: Once after a full moon: acute type A aortic dissection and lunar phases
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Do golfers really live longer than everybody else?
title: Golf: a game of life and death: reduced mortality in Swedish golf players
venue: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
note: A Swedish registry study reported lower mortality among golf federation members than expected from population rates. People selected themselves into golf, and the comparison does not identify a causal effect on lifespan.

headline: Did people who ate chocolate have fewer cases of atrial fibrillation?
title: Chocolate intake and risk of clinically apparent atrial fibrillation: the Danish Diet, Cancer, and Health Study
note: A Danish cohort recorded lower rates of clinically detected atrial fibrillation among people reporting moderate chocolate intake. The study estimated an association from self-reported diet and registry diagnoses.

headline: Does setting the clocks ahead cause a spike in car crashes?
title: Daylight Savings Time and Traffic Accidents
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: This brief original report found different collision counts around spring and autumn clock changes. Other analyses of the clock shift did not consistently find the same pattern. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8961329/

headline: Does eating spicy food really mean you live longer?
title: Consumption of spicy foods and total and cause specific mortality: population based cohort study
note: A large Chinese cohort reported lower mortality among people who reported eating spicy food more frequently. The estimate came from a comparison of dietary habits rather than a randomized intervention.

headline: Did nicotine patches help some patients with active ulcerative colitis?
title: Transdermal Nicotine for Active Ulcerative Colitis
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: This randomized trial found more remissions when nicotine patches were added to existing treatment than with placebo patches. Side effects were more common with nicotine.

headline: Does drinking more water slow chronic kidney disease?
title: Effect of Coaching to Increase Water Intake on Kidney Function Decline in Adults With Chronic Kidney Disease: The CKD WIT Randomized Clinical Trial
note: Urine volume increased with coaching, while the change in estimated kidney filtration at one year did not differ significantly from the control group.

headline: Can your birthday predict your lifetime medical diagnoses?
title: Birth month affects lifetime disease risk: a phenome-wide method
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
note: Electronic health records were screened for associations between month of birth and many diagnostic categories, including cardiovascular conditions.

headline: Do menstrual cycles temporarily synchronize with the moon?
title: Women temporarily synchronize their menstrual cycles with the luminance and gravimetric cycles of the Moon
note: The authors examined long-term menstrual records and reported intermittent alignment with lunar cycles.

headline: Can strangers praying for you change the outcome of heart surgery?
title: Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (STEP) in cardiac bypass patients: a multicenter randomized trial of uncertainty and certainty of receiving intercessory prayer
note: The trial found no improvement in complication-free recovery from prayer; participants certain that strangers were praying for them had more complications.

headline: Is surgery riskier on the surgeon's birthday?
title: Patient mortality after surgery on the surgeon’s birthday: observational study
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does the moon predict admission for bipolar disorder?
title: Is there an association between the lunar phases and hospital admission for different episode types in bipolar disorder? A retrospective study in northern China
note: The authors analyzed hospital records by lunar phase and reported fewer admissions around new and full moons.

headline: Does the moon have anything to do with heart failure admissions?
title: The impact of the moon cycles' in different seasons on heart failure patients' hospitalization and length of stay
note: The authors analyzed heart failure hospitalizations by lunar cycle and season, reporting an interaction involving lunar phase, summer and body mass index.

headline: Do people sleep later and less before the full moon?
title: Moonstruck sleep: Synchronization of human sleep with the moon cycle under field conditions
note: The authors used wrist activity measurements to relate sleep timing and duration to lunar phases in several communities.

headline: Does Christmas have a peak in cancer deaths?
title: Deaths and major biographical events: a study of all cancer deaths in Germany from 1995 to 2009
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Do redheads need more anesthetic?
title: Anesthetic requirement is increased in redheads
note: A small experiment compared anesthetic concentrations required to suppress a response to electrical stimulation in women with natural red or dark hair.

headline: Did a rapid extra dose of IV fluid raise mortality in this trial of critically ill children?
title: Mortality after Fluid Bolus in African Children with Severe Infection
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Among children with severe infection and impaired perfusion studied in the main trial stratum, the fluid-bolus groups had higher 48-hour mortality than the group without an immediate bolus.

headline: Could transfusing fewer patients with major stomach bleeding improve survival?
title: Transfusion Strategies for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: This randomized trial compared a lower and a higher hemoglobin threshold for transfusion. Six-week survival was higher with the lower threshold in the population studied.

headline: Did fetal-cell transplants beat sham brain surgery for Parkinson's disease?
title: Transplantation of Embryonic Dopamine Neurons for Severe Parkinson's Disease
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The main global rating after one year did not show an overall benefit. The authors reported differences in some measures among younger patients, and some recipients developed abnormal movements.

headline: Does switching on a spinal cord implant reduce disability more than leaving it off?
title: Effect of Spinal Cord Burst Stimulation vs Placebo Stimulation on Disability in Patients With Chronic Radicular Pain After Lumbar Spine Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial
note: In a blinded crossover trial among implanted patients, disability scores during active stimulation did not differ significantly from placebo stimulation.

headline: Did niacin improve the cholesterol numbers without preventing more heart events?
title: Niacin in Patients with Low HDL Cholesterol Levels Receiving Intensive Statin Therapy
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: In this trial niacin changed HDL and triglyceride levels, while the clinical composite did not improve compared with placebo on top of intensive statin therapy.

headline: Did a balloon pump improve survival after a heart attack with cardiogenic shock?
title: Intraaortic Balloon Support for Myocardial Infarction with Cardiogenic Shock
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: Thirty-day mortality did not differ significantly between the balloon-pump and control groups in the randomized trial.

headline: Did B vitamins lower a blood marker without preventing another heart attack?
title: Homocysteine Lowering and Cardiovascular Events after Acute Myocardial Infarction
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The trial lowered homocysteine with folic acid and vitamin B12 but did not find a reduction in its main cardiovascular outcome.

headline: Did taking vitamin D every day actually prevent broken bones in this large trial?
title: Supplemental Vitamin D and Incident Fractures in Midlife and Older Adults
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: In this ancillary VITAL trial among adults not recruited for deficiency, supplementation did not reduce total, nonvertebral, or hip fractures.

headline: Did daily aspirin give healthy older adults more years free of disability?
title: Effect of Aspirin on Disability-free Survival in the Healthy Elderly
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The randomized trial found no improvement in its composite measure of disability-free survival. Major bleeding was more frequent with aspirin.

headline: Did a ventilator strategy meant to protect the lungs increase ICU mortality?
title: High-Frequency Oscillation in Early Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The OSCILLATE trial stopped early after higher in-hospital mortality with early high-frequency oscillation. A separate trial did not find a statistically significant mortality difference. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1215716

headline: Did ivermectin make mild COVID-19 symptoms go away faster?
title: Effect of Ivermectin on Time to Resolution of Symptoms Among Adults With Mild COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial
note: This placebo-controlled study did not detect a significant difference in its primary outcome, time until symptoms resolved.

headline: Could hydroxychloroquine prevent COVID-19 after a documented exposure?
title: A Randomized Trial of Hydroxychloroquine as Postexposure Prophylaxis for Covid-19
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The randomized trial found no significant reduction in compatible or confirmed illness in the two weeks after exposure.

headline: Did a common painkiller shorten an episode of acute back pain?
title: Efficacy of paracetamol for acute low-back pain: a double-blind, randomised controlled trial
note: Recovery time was similar in the regular-dose, as-needed, and placebo arms of the PACE trial.

headline: Did glucosamine or chondroitin beat placebo for knee pain overall?
title: Glucosamine, Chondroitin Sulfate, and the Two in Combination for Painful Knee Osteoarthritis
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The trial did not find significant benefit for the supplements overall. An exploratory moderate-to-severe pain subgroup result favored the combination.

headline: Did hormone therapy really prevent a second round of heart trouble?
title: Randomized Trial of Estrogen Plus Progestin for Secondary Prevention of Coronary Heart Disease in Postmenopausal Women
note: The HERS randomized trial found no overall reduction in coronary events during follow-up among postmenopausal women with established coronary disease.

headline: Does chewing gum wake the gut up after bowel surgery?
title: Randomized clinical trial of postoperative chewing gum versus standard care after colorectal resection
note: In this multicenter randomized comparison, postoperative gum chewing did not reduce length of stay or show a clear improvement in bowel recovery under the care protocols studied. Previous smaller trials had reported faster recovery. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16490895/

headline: Did a small daily piece of dark chocolate really lower blood pressure?
title: Effects of Low Habitual Cocoa Intake on Blood Pressure and Bioactive Nitric Oxide: A Randomized Controlled Trial
note: A small trial reported a modest blood pressure reduction with dark chocolate compared with white chocolate. Later pooled work evaluated results across multiple cocoa interventions. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20584271/

headline: Can a thyroid pill improve the lab number without making patients feel better?
title: Thyroid Hormone Therapy for Older Adults with Subclinical Hypothyroidism
venue: The New England Journal of Medicine
note: The TRUST trial found that levothyroxine lowered thyroid-stimulating hormone. It did not improve the two main symptom and tiredness scores in the older adults studied.

headline: What does a copper bracelet do for rheumatoid arthritis?
title: Copper bracelets and magnetic wrist straps for rheumatoid arthritis—analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects: a randomised double-blind placebo controlled crossover trial
note: Participants took turns wearing a copper bracelet and wrist straps with different magnetic strengths, including a demagnetized strap. Neither copper nor magnetism produced a clinically meaningful reduction in pain or inflammation.

headline: Does the month you were born relate to cardiovascular mortality?
title: Birth month, birth season, and overall and cardiovascular disease mortality in US women: prospective cohort study
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does eating dark chocolate go with fewer depression symptoms?
title: Is there a relationship between chocolate consumption and symptoms of depression? A cross-sectional survey of 13,626 US adults
note: A cross-sectional dietary survey linked self-reported dark chocolate intake to lower odds of elevated depression questionnaire scores.

headline: Or do people with depression eat more chocolate?
title: Mood food: chocolate and depressive symptoms in a cross-sectional analysis
note: This cross-sectional analysis reported higher chocolate consumption among participants with higher depression symptom scores.
